The test image shows two tomato stems split longitudinally, revealing the lower stem and root region. Key features:
- Internal brown/tan vascular discoloration streaking up the stem
- Brown, deteriorated roots
- Outer stem still partially green at top
- No visible white mycelium or sclerotia
- Longitudinal cross-section showing internal tissue browning

This pattern of internal vascular browning in the lower stem strongly suggests a vascular wilt disease. Top candidates: **Verticillium_Wilt** (internal vascular browning) or **Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot** (stem rot at crown).

Let me view one reference image for Verticillium_Wilt to confirm.

The reference image for Verticillium_Wilt shows above-ground wilting symptoms (yellowing, drooping leaves). The test image, however, shows the classic diagnostic view: **longitudinal stem cross-sections** with brown vascular tissue discoloration, which plant pathologists use to confirm vascular wilt diseases. The brown streaking in the xylem tissue, combined with deteriorated roots, is the hallmark diagnostic evidence for Verticillium wilt - pathologists split the stem to show exactly this internal browning pattern.

The reference confirms this is the same disease, just shown from the diagnostic/internal perspective rather than above-ground symptom view.

No white mycelium (ruling out Sclerotinia/Southern Blight), no bacterial ooze (ruling out bacterial wilts). Verticillium_Wilt is the best match from the available classes."}
